level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: a large integer literal is automatically long. Right rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.
wrong rule: Java has no float literals. Right rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.
wrong rule: Java has no long literals. Right rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.
wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

Points to LT (each literal denotes one fixed value whose type is read from how it is written). Applied unevenly, a student reads 2.0 as an int in one place, or '7' as the number 7 in one expression and as a character in the next. (here mixing in: "a large integer literal is automatically long")
Rewriting a literal in another form keeps the value but changes the type, and so the operation: 10 / 3 is 3 but 10.0 / 3 is 3.333..., and "5" + 1 is "51" but 5 + 1 is 6.
wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice prints it only once. Right rule: Each expression in the output is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.

Applies the print rule (LT) unevenly: inserts a line break after a print on one line but not another, or drops a repeated value. (here mixing in: "An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once")
wrong rule: () are optional on a call with no argument. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses after the name.
Changing print to println (or back) moves the following output to a new line (or the same line) but keeps the characters printed; swapping two print statements swaps their text.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same (no newline difference). Right rule: println(s) prints s and then ends the line, but print(s) does not, so print("a"); print("b"); gives ab on one line.

Points to LT (output appears in the order the output calls execute, with a line break only after println). An uneven trace drops a repeated value, puts output lines out of order, or adds line breaks after print on some calls. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string to end the line.

wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once. Right rule: Every expression in the output is printed, so System.out.println(y + " " + x + " " + y) with x=6, y=9 prints 9 6 9.
Switching System.out.print/println to StdOut.print/println keeps the output. Changing println to print keeps every character but removes the line break, so lines join.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.
